title: When "isn't" means "is": じゃない and ではない
summary: じゃない is the negative of the copula, but as a question or an exclamation it means "isn't it?" or "well, it is!". It is a tag, like ね.

blocks.text: **じゃない** is a shortening of **ではない**, the negative of the copula だ / です. As a plain negative it just denies: これはペンじゃない, "This is not a pen". But in casual speech it often means the opposite.

Many languages ask for agreement with a negative: "It's nice, isn't it?". Japanese does too: さくらじゃないですか is "Isn't that Sakura?", and the speaker thinks it is. In casual speech か disappears, so the form stays and **tone** does the work. English does the same with tone alone: "She came on Saturday." / "She came on Saturday?" / "She came on Saturday?!"

rows: あれはさくらじゃない。
あれはさくらじゃない？

blocks.text: A tag that stretches to anything
As a tag, じゃない works like **ね**, on adjectives and verbs too. It is **not** the negative of the word before it. The true negative of 暑い is 暑くない.

blocks.en: I already told you, didn't I?

blocks.text: Even shorter and very casual: **じゃん**.

blocks.en: I told you yesterday, you know.

blocks.text: Politely, **のではないでしょうか** sums up an argument gently. The clause 間違っている is complete; **の** ("the case") makes it a noun, so ではない can join it; and でしょうか adds a soft question. Japanese writers prefer this gentle suggestion to a blunt assertion. In casual speech のではない shortens to んじゃない.

cars.text: その理論が間違っている
cars.label: complete clause

blocks.text: その理論が間違っているのではないでしょうか。

blocks.jp: その理論は間違っているのではないでしょうか。
blocks.en: Might that theory not be mistaken? (I think it is.)

items: **じゃない** = ではない (negative of だ).
Rising tone or exclamation: it means "isn't it? / well, it is!".
As a tag, じゃない ≈ ね; じゃん is its casual form.
Plain negatives of adjectives and verbs stay くない / ない.
